Lots of discussion here in the wake of the Mint hack about verifying the hash on your downloaded ISO, and how to verify that the hash itself hasn't been compromised, etc. Something I think got overlooked that I believe deserves more attention is bittorrent: most of the distros, Mint included, in addition to providing direct download links via several mirrors, will also provide a torrent file for seeding the ISO. Once the ISO is properly seeded, which literally takes mere minutes after a new release, poisoning that swarm of thousands of seeds is a far more difficult task than hacking a poorly-secured website and changing some files around in /var/www.

Your torrent software will do automatic checksum calculations against a huge group of existing ISOs as the file is being downloaded, and you can always do an md5sum check on your own once the download is complete, just for your own warm and fuzzy. It's secure; it's fast; and it saves the foundation on bandwidth. It really is the go-to solution for putting your mind at ease, whichever side of the distribution chain you happen to be on.

However if as in this case the website is compromised, the website links where changed to point to corrupted files. There is nothing about torrents that can stop someone from making a compromised torrent file, seeding it and changing the link to that.

True, but if you download a torrent for a Linux release that's been out for a few months, only to find that there's one seed, that's a pretty good indication something is wrong. One seed is not a swarm.

I think creating a legitimate-sized new swarm for the compromised torrent is much easier than hacking the site in the first place. With $50 you could already buy like 10 seedboxes to seed the compromised ISO... pretty much everyone would get the ISO downloaded with their connection's maximum download speed and it would not look suspicious at all to most people.

But how are you going to get clients into the swarm? You'd still have to hack the site to replace the legitimate torrent or magnet link with your fake. Now you're in the same situation, only you're spending money and you still don't have a swarm that looks legitimate -- you'd have to buy a couple hundred seed boxes to mimic the standard seed presence for Mint.

The hacker has experience with botnets; which could seed the ISO, and was able the change the Checksum on the official website to that of the backdoored ISO. I don't know much about what happened or what we could do, but the hacker seemed to have covered their bases.

EDIT: They also auctioned off a copy of the forums for 85 bucks. If the job costed them any more than that I'm sure that they would have charged the cost

  • the torrent/magnet links
  • the page hosting all this information
